email-raw-headers.description: Every header the message carried, folded away behind an expander and capped in height with its own scrollbar - a forwarded message can arrive with a hundred of them, and they must not push the body off the screen.

email-body-toolbar.title: Body View Toolbar
email-body-toolbar.description: Rendered / Plain text / HTML source, plus Open in browser. Each button is present only when the message actually has that form, and the active one is accented - so the toolbar states what a message contains as much as it switches between views.

email-body-modes.title: View Mode Buttons
email-body-modes.description: Switches the body pane between the rendered markdown, the raw plain-text part and the HTML source. A message opens on Rendered, whichever body parts it has.

email-open-browser.title: Open in Browser
email-open-browser.description: Writes the HTML body with its inline images to a temp file and opens it in the shell's browser tab - the full-fidelity view for a message the markdown rendering cannot do justice to. Offered only when there is an HTML body.
email-open-browser.note: Exports the HTML body to a temp file and hands it to the shell's WebView2 tab - a second live surface a unit test has no business spawning. That the button is offered only when there IS an HTML body falls out of HasHtmlBody, asserted on email-body-modes.

email-body.title: Body Pane
email-body.description: The message on its own surface card. An HTML body is converted to markdown with cid: inline images rewritten to local files so they actually appear; a message with only a plain-text part renders that instead, so the pane is never blank when there is something to show.

email-error.title: Parse Failure State
email-error.description: Replaces the whole message with the reason it could not be read. A mail file that fails to parse is common enough - truncated exports, unknown .msg variants - that a blank viewer would read as a broken feature.

email-attachment-strip.title: Attachment Strip
email-attachment-strip.description: One button per non-inline attachment, with its name, size and content type. Hidden entirely when there are none. Clicking one opens it in its own viewer through the virtual filesystem - the same path a double-click takes anywhere else - so a PDF attachment lands in the PDF viewer rather than being extracted by hand.

vdisk-ui.title: UI
vdisk-ui.description: The inspector tab: a metadata pane on the left describing the image and its volumes, the contents tree in the middle, and the action bar on the right. Read-only by design - it shows what is inside a disk image without opening anything out of it.
vdisk-ui.note: The UI journey here is the file-explorer route rather than a control sweep: the tab is three read-only panes with two buttons, and the interesting path is that double-clicking an image in the browser walks into it. Each pane is asserted against the view-model.

vdisk-functionality.title: Functionality
vdisk-functionality.description: What sits under the tab: reading a .vhd/.vhdx/.iso/.img superblock and filesystem through DiscUtils, exposing the image as a browsable container so the file explorer can walk into it, mounting it as a real drive letter, and the actions that open it here.

vdisk-metadata.title: Metadata Pane
vdisk-metadata.description: What the image is, before anything is browsed: format, partition scheme, total capacity, and a row per volume with its filesystem, label and used-of-total size.

vdisk-format-summary.title: Format Summary
vdisk-format-summary.description: Format, partition scheme and capacity, read from the superblock. An image the reader does not recognise says so rather than showing blanks - and says it only once the read has actually finished.

vdisk-volume-table.title: Volume Table
vdisk-volume-table.description: One row per volume: filesystem, label, used and total size. A partitioned image can carry several, and which one holds the data is the first thing anyone wants to know.

vdisk-contents-tree.title: Contents Tree
vdisk-contents-tree.description: The image's directory structure as an expand-aware flat row list, folders before files. A folder loads its children only when first opened - a disk image can hold a whole filesystem, and walking it up front would stall the tab. Activating a file does nothing at all: this tab inspects, it never launches.
vdisk-contents-tree.note: The read-only rule is asserted directly: activating a file row opens nothing, internally or through the shell. Content is reached by browsing the image in the file explorer instead, so a file inside a disk has one open path rather than two with different scopes.

vdisk-status.title: Busy / Status Line
vdisk-status.description: Says what the tab is doing - reading a directory, extracting - and carries the reason when one of those fails, so an error surfaces on the page rather than as a tab that stopped responding.

vdisk-action-bar.title: Action Bar
vdisk-action-bar.description: Extract and Mount, each enabled only when the image actually supports it.

vdisk-extract.title: Extract All
vdisk-extract.description: Writes the whole image out to a folder the user picks. Disabled until the image is recognised, and does nothing at all if the folder picker is cancelled.

vdisk-mount.title: Mount
vdisk-mount.description: Attaches the image as a real drive letter through the Windows virtual-disk API. Offered only for formats Windows can mount natively, and everything but an ISO needs elevation - which is why the mount runs through the privilege bridge rather than from the feature.
vdisk-mount.note: Attaching a drive letter is an elevated system call, so what is asserted is the gate rather than the effect: which formats offer the button at all, and which of those need elevation. The mount itself goes through the privilege bridge, not the feature.

vdisk-reader.title: Disk Image Reader
vdisk-reader.description: Reads .vhd, .vhdx, .iso and raw .img through DiscUtils: the partition table and volume descriptions, a directory's children, an entry's stat, and a file's bytes as a stream. Everything above this is format-agnostic.

vdisk-vfs.title: Disk as a Virtual Filesystem
vdisk-vfs.description: A disk image is a browsable container, so double-clicking one in the file explorer walks into it like a folder and its files open in their own viewers. Read-only: the handler advertises no write capability, and a file is materialised on demand rather than the whole image extracted.

vdisk-mount-service.title: Mount / Unmount
vdisk-mount-service.description: Attaching and detaching an image as a drive letter, and remembering which letters are image-backed so Unmount is offered on those drives and nowhere else. Everything but an ISO needs elevation.

vdisk-open-actions.title: Open Actions
vdisk-open-actions.description: 'As Disk' opens the inspector tab; Mount is a separate file action for the mountable experience; Unmount is a drive action, hidden for any path that is not an image-backed drive.

compressed-functionality.title: Functionality
compressed-functionality.description: What sits under the tab: the format backends that actually read and write each container, exposing an archive as a browsable folder so the file explorer can walk into it, and the file and folder actions that zip, unzip and open one.

product-ui.title: UI
product-ui.description: The three views over one product tree: the sunburst the tree is browsed and edited in, the integrity page that lists every broken snaplink, and the graph canvas over the product-plus-code knowledge graph. Two more views are planned; each is a panel here rather than a feature of its own, because they are views of the same data.

product-ai-act-product-lint.title: product_lint
product-ai-act-product-lint.description: Check the modelling rules - backbone, concerns by role, claims with nothing behind them. Advisory.

product-ai-act-product-add-node.title: product_add_node
product-ai-act-product-add-node.description: Add a child node with the default concerns attached, so it arrives lint-clean. Approval-gated.

product-ai-act-product-move-node.title: product_move_node
product-ai-act-product-move-node.description: Reparent a node and its subtree, refusing a cycle. Approval-gated.

product-ai-act-product-rename-node.title: product_rename_node
product-ai-act-product-rename-node.description: Change a node's id, retargeting parent, children and node snaplinks. Cannot reach a [CoversNode] in test source, and says so. Approval-gated.

product-ai-act-product-remove-node.title: product_remove_node
product-ai-act-product-remove-node.description: Delete a node, refusing one that still has children unless recursion is asked for. Approval-gated.

product-ai-act-product-remap.title: product_remap_snaplinks
product-ai-act-product-remap.description: Rewrite snaplink paths after a file moved - an exact path or a directory prefix. Approval-gated.

product-ai-act-product-doctor.title: product_doctor
product-ai-act-product-doctor.description: Check the tree's own structure - child ids resolve, parents list their children, no snaplink points into a linked worktree - and optionally repair it. Approval-gated.

product-report.title: Shared Report Rendering
product-report.description: One rendering of each query result - find, query, describe, tree, lint, validate - used by both the nexaflow-initiatives CLI and the in-app AI tools. They answer the same questions over the same services, so the answer has to read identically from both; keeping the text here is what stops the two drifting.

product-ai-context-sunburst.title: Sunburst context
product-ai-context-sunburst.description: The whole-product survey plus a zoom on the focused node: breadcrumb, status, concerns, snaplinks, children, and the faulted-items list. Not readiness-gated - the tree is loaded before the tab paints, so there is no window in which it would report an empty product.

product-ai-context-integrity.title: Integrity context
product-ai-context-integrity.description: The scan verdict and the broken snaplinks, capped at 30 with the remainder counted. Held until the first scan lands: a full scan tree-sitter-parses every referenced file and runs on the background queue, so an ungated send would report 'no issues' for a tree nobody has checked yet.

product-ai-context-graph.title: Graph context
product-ai-context-graph.description: The graph summary and the focused N-hop neighbourhood. Held until the graph.json load finishes, and distinguishes still-loading from failed-to-load, so neither reads as an empty graph.

sysinfo-ai-context-dashboard.title: Dashboard context
sysinfo-ai-context-dashboard.description: The device summary - CPU, memory, disks, GPU, OS build. Held until the WMI probe finishes, and released even when it fails, so a machine that will not answer does not hang the conversation.

sysinfo-ai-context-services.title: Services context
sysinfo-ai-context-services.description: Service counts by state and what is selected. Held until the service list has been gathered.

sysinfo-ai-context-envvars.title: Environment Variables context
sysinfo-ai-context-envvars.description: Variable counts per scope and the state of PATH - the one variable worth calling out, because a broken PATH is the usual reason someone is looking at this page at all.

processes-ai-context-list.title: Process list context
processes-ai-context-list.description: Process count, system CPU and memory, and the top consumers. Held until the first sample has landed - an ungated send would report a machine with no processes on it.

processes-ai-context-detail.title: Process detail context
processes-ai-context-detail.description: One process: its identity, resource use, threads, modules and handles. Ready once it has data OR once the process has exited - a process that is gone is describable as gone, and waiting for data that will never arrive would hang the send forever.

projects-ai-context-list.title: Project list context
projects-ai-context-list.description: The project count and which project is selected.
projects-ai-context-list.note: Thin: a count plus the selection. It omits the project's description and criteria, which the AI can still reach through the read tools.

projects-ai-context-detail.title: Project detail context
projects-ai-context-detail.description: The open project's name and backlog count.
projects-ai-context-detail.note: Thin: name plus a backlog count, with no item detail. Worth widening before this is called done - the page is showing a backlog the context does not describe.

aichat-ai-context-conversation.title: Conversation context
aichat-ai-context-conversation.description: The hub: assembles each pinned page's context (a file-system page augmented with a live listing), the attachment contents, any prior analysis standing in for older messages, then the budgeted history. Readiness-gated on every pinned page, so one page still loading holds the whole send.

aichat-ai-context-browser.title: Browser context
aichat-ai-context-browser.description: The saved-conversation list: how many there are, the active date filter and which conversation is selected. Not readiness-gated - the list is loaded before the tab paints.

product-ai-act-tree.title: Product tree commands
product-ai-act-tree.description: Everything the nexaflow-initiatives CLI does to the tree: navigate (find / query / tree / zoom / survey / needs-attention), check (validate / lint / doctor), edit (status, description, concerns, snaplinks) and restructure (add / move / rename / remove / remap).

product-ai-act-graph.title: Knowledge graph commands
product-ai-act-graph.description: The code-discovery surface: the product tree crossed with the whole-repo AST and the snaplinks between them. Answers what a text search cannot - who calls or instantiates a type, what a change's neighbourhood is, and which product feature owns a given piece of code.

product-ai-act-view.title: Graph view commands
product-ai-act-view.description: The two tools that act on what the graph canvas is *rendering* rather than on the model - which node is centred and what is visible. The only view-specific tools on the whole Product surface; everything else means the same thing from any of the three views.

product-ai-act-graph-search.title: graph_search
product-ai-act-graph-search.description: Find graph nodes by id or label, best match first - an exact label, then a prefix, then a substring. The starting point for every other graph call, since they all take a node id.

product-ai-act-graph-context.title: graph_context
product-ai-act-graph-context.description: Everything about one node in a single call: what it is, its source, its relationships in both directions, and the product feature(s) that own it. The one to reach for before reading a file.

product-ai-act-graph-node.title: graph_node
product-ai-act-graph-node.description: One node and every edge touching it, both directions, grouped by relationship - who it calls and who calls it - plus its hyperedges.

product-ai-act-graph-walk.title: graph_walk
product-ai-act-graph-walk.description: Every node within N hops, grouped by distance - the neighbourhood around a change and what it might affect.

product-ai-act-graph-grep.title: graph_grep
product-ai-act-graph-grep.description: Search the source of nodes near a starting node. The thing a plain text search cannot do, because it has no notion of 'near' - scoping a regex to a type's neighbourhood finds the callers that matter instead of every file sharing a word.

product-ai-act-graph-code.title: graph_code
product-ai-act-graph-code.description: The source block a code node points at - the member or type itself, not the whole file.

product-ai-act-graph-stats.title: graph_stats
product-ai-act-graph-stats.description: The shape of the graph: node counts by type and the commonest relationships. Worth a call before a big exploration.

product-ai-act-graph-build.title: graph_build
product-ai-act-graph-build.description: Rebuild graph.json from the tree and the current source. Incremental - only changed files are re-parsed - but it still walks the repo, so it is the one graph tool that costs real time and the only one that writes. Approval-gated.
product-ai-act-graph-build.note: The build itself is asserted by GraphBuilderTests and GraphCacheTests, which is where the incremental cache and the byte-determinism live. What the tool adds is the approval gate and the 'no graph yet - build one' path, and that is what its own test covers.

product-graph-query.title: Graph Query & Rendering
product-graph-query.description: Reading a built graph - search, one node's neighbourhood, the one-shot context view, an N-hop walk, and grep over the source of nearby nodes - plus one rendering of each result. Shared by the nexaflow-initiatives CLI and the in-app assistant, so both answer identically; the search ranking and the block-end scan that decides where a member's source stops both live here rather than in either caller.

tabular-chart-view.title: Chart view
tabular-chart-view.description: NOT YET BUILT. Plot the loaded columns rather than only reading them - pick a numeric column (or two) against a category or time column and draw it beside the grid. The pieces already exist: column typing knows which columns are numeric or temporal, and Visuals.Common already owns chart primitives. Must respect the windowed reader: a chart over a file too large to load has to be built from a scan rather than from the loaded rows.

page-search.title: Page Search (? / ISearchable)
page-search.description: The shell's one search route. A page ViewModel declares ISearchable and the '?' handler routes AI-bar searches to it - no per-feature query handler and no registration. SearchSyntax parses ?/pattern/flags centrally so regex is a mode of search the user declares, not something inferred from punctuation; the page receives an already-decided SearchRequest. A page that cannot run regex sets SupportsRegex=false and MUST return SearchOutcome.Unsupported rather than falling back to a literal scan.

page-search-conformance.title: Search conformance
page-search-conformance.description: The shared test suite every ISearchable implementor must pass. Its purpose is one specific silent failure: a page that appears to support regular expressions but runs a literal Contains, showing the user confidently wrong results. Each implementor derives a [TestClass] from SearchableConformanceTests; guard tests run the suite against deliberately broken fakes to prove it actually rejects them.

page-search-ai-tools.title: Agent search tools
page-search-ai-tools.description: Any ISearchable page automatically exposes two client tools, added by AIService rather than by the feature. search_page reads matches and returns them to the model WITHOUT changing what the user sees; show_search_results narrows the visible set to ids from that read. Split deliberately so the agent can search broadly, filter by meaning, and only then show the user what survived.

search-browser-route.title: Browser search (? / ISearchable)
search-browser-route.description: The file browser answers '?' by searching the folder tree it is showing - so '?' has exactly ONE owner across the app. Displaying results is a HandleObject handoff of a FileSearchRequest: whichever feature owns file search claims it and presents a Search tab, and the browser never learns which, exactly as the scratchpad hands off a clicked URL. The agent's read path needs hits back rather than a tab, so it goes through the discovered IFileCorpusSearch engine instead. Scoring overrides the term-count default with the shared glob/property-filter scorer, damping a bare absolute path so '>' navigation still wins it.

page-search-regex.title: Regex everywhere
page-search-regex.description: Regex is a mode of search available on EVERY searchable page - there is deliberately no per-page opt-out, because a capability that varies page to page is worse than none. A backend whose query language has no regex operator (Windows Search AQS) translates the pattern into the widest query still covering it and re-filters the rows with the real regex: widening only over-matches, so the post-filter restores exact semantics and translation quality affects speed rather than correctness. Post-filtering needs the matched text, and a file index returns names rather than file bodies - so a regex over a file corpus is scoped to the file name, stated via SearchOutcome.Narrowed so a content-intent pattern never comes back as a bare zero.

search-verify.title: Two-stage content verification
search-verify.description: Content regex over a file index, answered in two stages because AQS can narrow by name but cannot evaluate a pattern against file contents. Stage one returns index rows immediately: those whose NAME matches the regex are already proven and need no file read, the rest are shown as candidates with a question-mark overlay. Stage two reads the candidates on a background sweep and settles each row in place - tick, or struck through then removed when the pass completes. Past 50 candidates the sweep is opt-in: the first 50 run anyway so the list is usable, and a banner offers the rest rather than reading thousands of files off the back of a keystroke. Content comes from a format-aware IFileTextExtractor when some feature provides one for that type, else the file is read as text (BOM/encoding sniffed, binaries skipped, size capped).
search-verify.note: Row states are five-way, and the split is about EVIDENCE not just outcome. Verified = name matched, or content matched in a file we decoded properly. Uncertain = the pattern WAS found, but by scanning the raw bytes of a format we don't understand - real, possibly incidental, like a plain-text scan finding 'magic' in a JPEG tag. Rejected = read as proper text and not there (conclusive). Unreadable = couldn't open it, OR not found in raw bytes of a container whose real text is compressed - absence there proves nothing, so it must never be reported as a miss. Candidate = not yet checked. An unknown file type is never skipped: it is always scanned as text, and only the CONFIDENCE differs. Unreadable and Uncertain are never re-offered for checking, since re-reading gives the same answer and makes the button look dead.

search-aqs.title: AQS property terms
search-aqs.description: Advanced Query Syntax property constraints (kind:document, author:john, size:>1mb, modified:last week) accepted as one more term kind alongside globs, patterns and text - the syntax people already know from Explorer's search box, and the part this feature previously hand-rolled worst (two regexes covering a fraction of it, no relative dates, no localisation). Translated by Windows' own AQS parser (ISearchQueryHelper.GenerateSQLFromUserQuery) behind IAqsTranslator, so which token is a constraint, how terms combine and what SQL comes out all stay testable without the Windows Search service. A structured term is INDEX-ENFORCED: the post-filter must never re-test it, since nothing in a filename or a file's text can answer 'size:>1mb'. The COM interop is a hand-transcribed vtable from the SDK header - the published docs list members alphabetically - so it is additionally proved by an Interactive-category test that calls the real service.
search-aqs.note: Parsed ONCE into a SearchCondition tree (IQueryParser -> IQuerySolution.Resolve), then projected twice: SearchConditionSql for the index, SearchConditionEvaluator for the folder walk. Resolve is mandatory - without it values come back untyped (a size is unreadable text, a relative date is a phrase) - and its reference-time argument is [ref], so passing null fails the whole resolve. The legacy SearchQueryParser.Parse(string) overload still carries the old size:/date: regexes; they no longer serve any user-typed query (those go through terms + AQS) but remain the only implementation behind that string entry point.

win-search-folder-scan.title: Manual folder scan
win-search-folder-scan.description: When the Windows index has no answer - it returned nothing, or the service is unreachable - the banner offers a manual walk of the location rather than showing a bare empty list. An index that never covered a folder returning nothing is not an answer to the user's question, but a tree scan reads every file and can run for minutes, so it is offered and never started automatically. The scan applies the SAME parsed terms as the index path: name-side terms (globs, property constraints) filter first so a file ruled out by its name is never opened, and anything still undecided is settled by reading the file. Hits stream into the list as they are found and arrive already verified, so unlike the index path there is no second pass. Cancellable, and a stopped scan reports its count as a floor rather than a total.

win-search-coverage.title: Index coverage
win-search-coverage.description: Reads the Windows indexer's crawl scope (ISearchCrawlScopeManager) to say how much of a location it actually covers - not indexed, partially indexed, or fully indexed - so an empty result can be reported as what it means rather than as 'not found'. The banner is worded from that: an unindexed folder offers the manual scan outright, a partially indexed one warns that results may be incomplete, and a fully indexed one distinguishes 'these came from the index' from 'the index found nothing here'. Strictly read-only: every mutating method on the COM interface is left undeclared, so this explains the machine's indexing configuration and never changes it. The AI gets an index_coverage command returning the crawl-scope rules for a path, so a user can ask why something isn't indexed.

code-find.title: Search ? support
code-find.description: The As Code editor answers the shell's '?' search by declaring ISearchable. The scan lives on the shared FileTextEditorViewModel, so the plain editor answers identically; matches are painted by the shared SearchHighlightRenderer and counted in the status bar, and the agent can narrow the set through ShowResultsAsync.

markdown-find.title: Find in the open document
markdown-find.description: The markdown editor answers '?' against whatever surface is showing — the source box when open, the rendered text otherwise — and never switches the view. A source match is selected in the source box; a rendered match is highlighted in place by the shared RenderedMarkdownSearch. The agent's non-display search reads the document source. Whole-word matching with *wildcards* (fig*, *fig, *fig*, f?g) comes from the central SearchTerm contract.

email-find.title: Search ? Support
email-find.description: The email viewer answers '?' over what the message currently shows: the body pane on screen, the raw headers only while that list is open, and every attachment — by name, by the text inside it, and recursively into any message/rfc822 it carries. A body match is highlighted (rendered) or selected (text pane); a matching header row and attachment tile light up. Each hit says where it came from. ShowResultsAsync declines — a message has no list to narrow.

log-viewer-search.title: Search (?)
log-viewer-search.description: The log tab as an ISearchable page: '?' scans the whole loaded document through the shared TextSearchMatcher, paints matches with its own SearchMatchRenderer, and steps through them from the status-bar chip. A third, independent layer - it neither reads nor writes the regex fade-filter or the custom highlight term, which mean different things. While the head is still streaming in the outcome carries a caveat, and the search re-runs when the head lands or the live tail appends.

page-search-chip.title: Search status chip
page-search-chip.description: The one search chip every ISearchable page shows: match count, the query as typed, previous/next stepping and dismiss. A single Visuals.Common control bound BY CONVENTION to the page ViewModel's own search state (IsSearchActive / SearchMatchCount / CurrentSearchTerm / HasSearchMatches and the three commands), with AutomationIds composed from a PagePrefix so each page keeps its own ids. Nothing at compile time proves the binding still reaches a page, so SearchStatusChipTests is the proof.

tabular-search.title: Search (?)
tabular-search.description: The grid as an ISearchable page. A hit is a ROW: the query is pushed into IRowSource.GetVisibleAsync as a cross-column predicate, so one existing call scans the whole file with no new IO API and no index. Composes with (never replaces) the typed per-column filters - a column filter is per-column and typed, while '?' asks whether ANY cell matches. ShowResultsAsync pins the grid to the agent's chosen absolute row indices. Past the scan cap the count is reported as a floor with a message and a '+' on the chip, never as a silent total.

io-vfs-mounts.title: Pass-through mounts
io-vfs-mounts.description: A virtual prefix (::id) mapped onto a real directory, resolved by string substitution with no temp extraction - so a mounted location is exactly as capable as the folder behind it while never revealing where that is. Distinguished from an archive entry by VirtualBacking, which decides whether an action needing the file's neighbours may run.

winfs-thispc-providers.title: Provided items
winfs-thispc-providers.description: Rows contributed by IThisPcItemProvider implementations, appended after the real drives and deduped against them. A local-path row is published as a pass-through mount, so the user browses it as a place of its own - Up walks back to This PC and the real folder is never shown.

json-search.title: Search (?)
json-search.description: The JSON tab as an ISearchable page. A small document is scanned in memory; a windowed one is streamed off the UI thread through JsonFileLoader.LoadVirtualChunkAsync, so '?' searches the whole FILE rather than the few hundred realised nodes. A hit is the top-level item whose subtree contains the match, identified by its depth-1 index - the one id that survives window eviction. The scan records each match's chunk offset so revealing a hit thousands of items away seeks straight to it instead of crawling forward a batch at a time. Orthogonal to the '$' JSONPath handler, which answers a structural address rather than a text query.

onedrive.title: OneDrive
onedrive.description: Surfaces the OneDrive sync folders already configured on this machine as This PC rows, each backed by a pass-through mount so the user browses it as a place of its own and never sees where OneDrive put it. Detection only - no OAuth, no Graph API, nothing to expire.

onedrive-detect.title: Detection
onedrive-detect.description: Reads HKCU Software/Microsoft/OneDrive/Accounts for accounts with a local sync folder. Skips the FileCoAuth bookkeeping key and accounts syncing nowhere; names rows as Explorer does. Falls back to the OneDrive environment variables only when the registry is silent, since they would otherwise duplicate what it found.

onedrive-provider.title: This PC rows
onedrive-provider.description: Turns detected accounts and hand-added folders into IThisPcItemProvider rows, applying the user's renames and hides. Memoised briefly because This PC redraws often; a config change cuts through the memo.

onedrive-options.title: Options
onedrive-options.description: This feature's own custom-control editor: detected folders listed alongside hand-added ones, renameable and hideable, with an Add folder picker. Records an override only where the user departed from what was detected.

onedrive-ui.title: UI
onedrive-ui.description: Where the user sees and steers this feature: the rows themselves are rendered by the file browser, so what belongs to OneDrive is its Options page.

onedrive-functionality.title: Functionality
onedrive-functionality.description: Finding the sync folders this machine already has, and offering them as This PC rows. Detection only - nothing here signs in or calls a cloud API.

onedrive-ai.title: AI Integration
onedrive-ai.description: Deliberately none. A sync folder is mounted as an ordinary browsable location, so the AI reads and writes it through the file browser's existing tools; a OneDrive-specific surface would only duplicate them. Revisit if cloud-API browsing lands, where listing without downloading would be a genuinely different capability.

font-search.title: Search (?)
font-search.description: The font tab as an ISearchable page: '?' matches the name of every font in the comparison list, marks the hits and steps the selection through them from the status-bar chip. The one searchable list that does NOT filter - the list IS the comparison, so hiding the rows that missed would take away what the user is comparing against. Hit ids are the 1-based indices the AI tools and get_context already use to name a font, so a search result round-trips straight into get_font_details. Adding or removing a font drops the search rather than renumbering stale positions.

processes-search.title: Search (?)
processes-search.description: The process list as an ISearchable page. '?' drives the toolbar search box the tab already had - same five fields (name, PID, company, description, image path), same flat-match-list presentation - but parsed by the shared query parser, so regex, quoted phrases and prefix wildcards mean here what they mean in a text tab. The box shows the query it was given, so an AI-run search is visible and dismissible; typing in the box drops the compiled pattern behind it. ShowResultsAsync pins the list to the agent's chosen PIDs, and the pin survives the 1s refresh tick.

processes-detail-search.title: Search (?) - details page
processes-detail-search.description: The per-process inspector as an ISearchable page, scoped to the sub-tab on screen: thread ids on Threads, module name and path on Modules, the handle name on Handles. Scoping is what makes one query box work on a page showing five different things - a search sweeping all three lists would report matches on tabs the user cannot see. Switching section drops the search rather than re-applying a TID pattern to module paths. Handles report honestly that they need their one admin-approved read before they can be searched, and General/Performance say where to search instead rather than failing. Answers by filtering through per-section ICollectionViews, so the 1s refresh tick reconciles underneath without losing the filter.

win-registry-search.title: Search (?)
win-registry-search.description: The registry tab as an ISearchable page: '?' walks the hive the tab has open - key names, value names and value data - the way regedit's Find does, and the chip steps the tree through the results. A hit is a KEY, not a value, because a key is the only thing the tree can navigate to; several matching values in one key collapse to one hit whose preview names the first, and landing there also selects that value row. Scoped to the tree's base, so a tab pinned at a key searches that subtree rather than silently widening to the whole hive. The walk runs off the UI thread and is bounded by a visited-key cap and a hit cap, reporting a truncated total as a floor with a '+' rather than as an exact number.

compressed-search.title: Search (?)
compressed-search.description: The archive inspector as an ISearchable page: '?' searches the manifest - every entry at every depth, whether or not its folder is open - and narrows the tree to the hits plus the folders above them, expanded. An entry matches on its NAME or its PATH inside the archive, one rule, which is what makes '?docs/guide' work and what makes naming a folder answer with that folder and its contents. Filename globs are understood ('?*.md') and judged against the entry name, never the path. No scan cap and no background thread: the manifest is already in memory because the tab read it to draw the tree; only the hit list handed to the agent is capped, and the count stays the true total. Rewriting the archive (add/recompress) drops the search rather than leaving rows pointing at entries that no longer exist.

vdisk-search.title: Search (?)
vdisk-search.description: The disk inspector as an ISearchable page: '?' searches the files and folders inside the image, by name or path within it, with filename globs judged against the name. It WALKS the image rather than the rows on screen - the contents tree is lazy, so filtering what is loaded would answer 'is it in the folders you happened to open' and its empty result would read as 'not in this image'. The walk runs off the UI thread, breadth-first (under a cap the shallow matches are the ones worth keeping), bounded by a folder cap and a hit cap, and reports a truncated total as a floor with a '+'. Results are shown by rebuilding the tree from the hits plus their folder spine, expanded - which is why dismissing the search re-reads the root: the filtered tree is a different tree, not a hidden subset.

sysinfo-search.title: Search (?)
sysinfo-search.description: The device dashboard as an ISearchable page: '?' matches the facts on the cards - each row's label and its value - and marks the ones that hit. The one searchable page that neither filters nor steps: the dashboard is a fixed set of cards the user is READING, not a list they are looking through, so hiding the rows that missed would take away the card they were shown, and there is no selection to step with. A hit id is 'Section/Label', the way a person names a fact, so a result round-trips. Re-gathering replaces every fact object and drops the marks with them.

sysinfo-services-search.title: Search (?)
sysinfo-services-search.description: The Services page as an ISearchable page. '?' drives the filter box the tab already had, over the same two fields (service name, display name), but parsed by the shared query parser - so regex, quoted phrases and prefix wildcards mean here what they mean in a text tab. One box and not two: the query the AI ran is visible in it, dismissible from the chip, and dropped the moment the user types over it. ShowResultsAsync pins the list to the agent's chosen service names.

sysinfo-envvars-search.title: Search (?)
sysinfo-envvars-search.description: The Environment Variables page as an ISearchable page: '?' matches a variable's NAME OR ITS VALUE and drives the filter box the tab already had, parsed by the shared query parser - so regex, quoted phrases and prefix wildcards mean here what they mean in a text tab. The value is in because it is what people are looking for ('which variable still has the old SDK path in it'), and the typed box matches the same two fields for the same reason: a box filtering by a narrower rule than '?' would give the same string two different answers depending on where it was typed. A row whose VALUE matched looks like any other in a list of names, so the hit preview carries the value. Scoped to the scope on screen - switching User/Machine drops the search rather than describing rows that are gone.

projects-search.title: Search (?)
projects-search.description: The project list as an ISearchable page: '?' matches a project's name, its folder name and its DESCRIPTION, and narrows the list to what matched. The description is in on purpose - a folder is something someone typed in a hurry, where what the project is about is written in the description, and 'the one about the invoice importer' is how anyone actually looks for one. Scoped to the bucket on screen (Projects / Shelf / Archives), so switching bucket drops the search. The selection follows the filter, so the summary pane never describes a project the list no longer shows; hit ids are folder names, the id read_project already speaks.

projects-detail-search.title: Search (?)
projects-detail-search.description: The project detail tab as an ISearchable page: '?' searches the BACKLOG - each item's title and its markdown detail - and narrows the board to what matched. The backlog and not the description, because the backlog is the list: it is the thing that grows to eighty items and needs finding things in, where the description is one document already on screen. A search run from the Project Details tab switches to Backlog - answering about a list the user cannot see would be worse than not answering. Hit ids are item ids, the id read_backlog_item already speaks.

aichat-search.title: Search (?)
aichat-search.description: The conversation browser as an ISearchable page: '?' searches the saved conversations - their titles AND the text of every message in them - and lists the ones that matched. Message text because a title is a generated slug nobody remembers; 'the chat where we worked out the retry backoff' is how anyone looks for one. The search deliberately IGNORES the date filter: it defaults to the last 7 days, so searching inside it would quietly answer 'did we discuss this recently' and its empty result would read as 'we never discussed this'. Dismissing the search, or picking a new date range, hands the filter back. Hit ids are conversation ids, so a result opens straight into the conversation tab.

aichat-conversation-search.title: Search (?)
aichat-conversation-search.description: One open conversation as an ISearchable page: '?' matches the text of every message in the thread - the user's and the assistant's - marks the bubbles that hit, and steps the view through them from the chip. It MARKS rather than filters: a thread is read in order, so hiding the messages that missed would leave replies with nothing to reply to and answers with no question above them. A hit id is its position in the thread, because a rendered assistant bubble carries text and not an id - so any rebuild (a load, a rewind) drops the search rather than renumbering onto bubbles that were never matched. Tool batches, approvals and the live activity line are machinery, not something that was said, and are not searched.

notebook-search.title: Search (?)
notebook-search.description: The notebook as an ISearchable page: '?' searches every cell's source - markdown and code alike - marks the cells that matched and steps the view through them, the way the code viewer does for a file. The difference from a code file is that a notebook is not one buffer, so A HIT IS A CELL: the cell is the only thing the page can scroll to and the id read_cell already takes, so several matches inside one cell collapse to one hit. Nothing is filtered - a notebook is read in order and cells build on the ones above them - and inside a CODE cell the matched words themselves are washed (CodeBlockView.Highlights), where a markdown cell renders to a document whose offsets are not the source's and carries the cell mark alone.

scratchpad-search.title: Search (?)
scratchpad-search.description: The board as an ISearchable page: '?' matches a post-it's content, HIDES the notes that missed, hands each survivor the query so its own body paints the matched words (the shared rendered-markdown painter, via InlineMarkdownEditor.FindInRendered), and pans the canvas to each hit in turn. Hiding rather than marking is what a corkboard needs - the notes are scattered across an infinite canvas at whatever zoom the user left it, so a mark on a note two screens away is a mark nobody sees. Panning and not zooming: the scale is the user's, and quietly refitting would lose the working view they set up. Steps in reading order (top row first, then left to right) rather than creation order. The recycle bin is out of scope - a binned note is not on the board.

product-search-page.title: Search Results
product-search-page.description: The graph search results page (page kind 'ProductSearch'): one query run over the WHOLE knowledge graph - node names and the source behind them - with each result openable where it actually lives. A page of its own rather than a filter on the sunburst, because the sunburst draws the product tree and the graph is that tree crossed with the whole repo: a result may be a feature, a type, a file or a line of code, and three of those have nowhere to sit on a sunburst. Two passes kept apart: NAME matches through the graph's own ranked search (exact label, then prefix, then substring), and SOURCE matches through a grep across every code node - the expensive half, and the reason the whole thing runs off the UI thread with a cap reported as a floor. The tab is identified by the product root alone, so searching twice re-points the one results tab instead of stacking a tab per query.

product-search-drillin.title: Drill into a result
product-search-drillin.description: Where a result goes when it is opened. A product node focuses the SUNBURST on it (the same 'node' deep link the Integrity page uses); anything with a file behind it is handed to the shell's default handler, so a .cs opens wherever a .cs normally opens and the results page never second-guesses that. A separate 'In graph' button selects the node in the GRAPH viewer, because 'where does this sit' is a different question from 'take me to it' - it passes a new one-shot 'node' param, dropped from the tab's identity so a second click re-points the one graph tab rather than opening another. A row with neither a product node nor a file hides its open button rather than offering a dead one.

product-search.title: Search (?)
product-search.description: The Product tab as an ISearchable page: '?' searches the whole knowledge graph and opens the results as their own tab rather than filtering the sunburst - the sunburst draws the product tree, and three quarters of what the graph can match (types, files, source lines) has nowhere to sit on it. The tab's own answer to the agent is the node-NAME half only, reported as Narrowed with a message saying the results page additionally greps the source, so a name-only count is never mistaken for the whole answer. A regex is handed over in the shared syntax so it survives the trip to the results page.

executable-inspector.title: Executable Inspector
executable-inspector.description: PE inspector for .exe/.dll/.sys: headers and sections, imports/exports, dependency graph, resources, decoded manifest, .NET metadata, embedded strings, and a signature/entropy/antivirus analysis. Opened by the 'Inspect' file action.

ui-2.title: UI
ui-2.description: Eight left-rail sections over one parsed image: Overview, Imports/Exports, Dependencies, Resources, Manifest, .NET, Strings, Analysis.

functionality-2.title: Functionality
functionality-2.description: Nexaflow.IO.Pe — a WPF-free, never-throwing PE reader: headers, sections, imports/exports, resources, version info, relocations, TLS, debug, CLR metadata, entropy and Authenticode.

ai-integration.title: AI Integration
ai-integration.description: GetContext summarises structure, entropy, signature and diagnostics; flagged Medium risk because every string in it is attacker-controlled.

pdf.title: PDF
pdf.description: Reading PDFs in Nexaflow: a reader tab that renders the document through the shared browser host with none of a browser's framing, a side panel of the document's own properties and table of contents, an AI tool surface over the same PdfPig readers that power search, and image extraction to a folder. No OCR - an image-only scan legitimately has no text, which is why the AI can look at a page as a picture instead.

pdf-search.title: Search text extraction
pdf-search.description: IFileTextExtractor for .pdf: page words plus title/author/subject/keywords, bookmark titles and filled-in form values. Empty string means read-it-and-there-is-no-text (a confident non-match); null means could-not-read (falls back to the raw byte scan).

pdf-extract-images.title: Extract Images
pdf-extract-images.description: IFileAction on the /document/pdf experience: pick a target folder, then a shell background task writes each distinct embedded image into a subfolder per document. JPEG/JPEG2000 pass through unre-encoded; everything else is decoded to PNG; repeats are dropped by content hash.

pdf-image-filters.title: Image codec filters
pdf-image-filters.description: PdfPig ships DCTDecode/JBIG2Decode/JPXDecode as unsupported stubs, each real decoder in its own package. PdfFilterProvider decorates the default table with them, which is what makes a scanned document yield extractable images at all.

pdf-functionality.title: Functionality
pdf-functionality.description: Reading PDFs: text for search, images for extraction. No viewer, so the feature has no UI of its own beyond the action-strip button the file browser draws.

graph-expandable-nodes.title: Expandable Nodes
graph-expandable-nodes.description: Expansion as a property of the graph model: a node can hide a subtree and offer a [+]/[-] chip as a SECOND hit region, independent of its click target. Driven by the config: nexaflow: front-matter block (expandDepth / maxFanOut / collapsed / expanded), which stock mermaid ignores. Unclaimed by the host, the diagram opens the node itself; claimed, the host re-emits (the PE inspector re-walks).

win-cux-tab-reuse.title: Tab Reuse on Open
win-cux-tab-reuse.description: Opening a page that is already open reuses that tab instead of adding another: ShellServices matches on PageKind plus the IDENTITY params the registration declares (PageParameter.Identity), then re-points the hit through IPageView.Reinitialize and records where it now looks. Params marked Identity:false locate a view INSIDE the document - Hex's offset/length - so repeatedly jumping from the PE inspector re-seeks one tab rather than stacking one per offset. Undeclared params stay identity; an inRightPane open deliberately skips all of this and always makes a fresh tab, which is how you get two views of one file.

hex-read-failure.title: Unreadable File Recovery
hex-read-failure.description: A file the viewer cannot read says so instead of painting zeroes. Every read path in HexBuffer has a 'return 0' escape that is indistinguishable from a file genuinely full of 0x00, so the buffer records WHY it gave up - missing, access denied, locked by another program, or stopped delivering bytes mid-read - and the tab asks the user in plain words whether to Retry (the lock may have gone) or Close tab. Retry re-opens from scratch; the failure is reported once per episode, not once per repaint, and never from inside a paint.

network.title: Network
network.description: Network adapter list, layered LAN device discovery into one correlated device graph, device actions, connectivity tools and a topology view. Discovery layers ship as lazily-loaded subfeature plugins; protocols themselves are DynamicProtocol documents rather than compiled code.

network-discovery.title: Discovery
network-discovery.description: Layered probes contributing observations to the device graph. ARP/neighbour table is a compiled plugin; higher layers are protocol documents.

network-graph.title: Device graph
network-graph.description: Identity lattice, provenanced facts, edges, staleness. Two different MACs never merge; an IP on new hardware is rebound, not merged.

network-protocol.title: DynamicProtocol
network-protocol.description: A protocol is a graph, written as JSON, and the engine holds no protocol specifics. Values become octets and back by a demand-driven walk over that graph: one description serves both directions, and where they differ it says so. An AI authors a description, a person reviews it, and a trusted one becomes a button on a device's page.
network-protocol.note: Ten corpus protocols round-trip byte-exact against real captures. NOT yet consumed by anything: the engine is referenced only by Nexaflow.Tests.IO, so nothing in the shell can reach it. Wants sub-nodes once it has a consumer - engine, definitions and the reviewing surface are three different things being tracked as one leaf.

network-guard.title: Send guard
network-guard.description: The only code that owns a socket. Target allow-list, volume ceilings, trust states, audit. Containment is structural: the protocol engine has no socket API in scope.

windowsapps-modify.title: Modify
windowsapps-modify.description: Reopens a Win32 program's own installer in maintenance mode so the user can add or remove features - Add/remove programs' 'Modify'. Offered only when the entry registered a ModifyPath (or is a Windows Installer product, where msiexec /I{ProductCode} is synthesised) and didn't set NoModify.

windowsapps-move.title: Move
windowsapps-move.description: Store apps only: relocates the package's files to another drive. Opens the Advanced Options pane with its Move card called out, since that is where the drive picker lives.

windowsapps-advanced.title: Advanced Options
windowsapps-advanced.description: A resizable right-hand pane for a Store app, mirroring Windows' Advanced options page: app identity, the background-execution dropdown, Terminate / Repair / Reset, a move-to-another-drive picker, and the app's add-ons. Opened from the row menu; closes back to a full-width list.

windowsapps-advanced-background.title: Background Permission
windowsapps-advanced-background.description: The 'Let this app run in background' tri-state - Power optimized / Always / Never - read from and written to the per-user BackgroundAccessApplications policy key Windows itself uses.

windowsapps-advanced-terminate.title: Terminate
windowsapps-advanced-terminate.description: Stops the package's running processes, identified by an image path inside the package's install folder. Reports how many were killed.

windowsapps-advanced-repair.title: Repair
windowsapps-advanced-repair.description: Re-registers the package from its own manifest, rebuilding its registration without touching the data the app saved.

windowsapps-advanced-reset.title: Reset
windowsapps-advanced-reset.description: Stops the app, deletes its state folders under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages, then re-registers it so it starts as if freshly installed. Destructive - confirmation-gated, and honest about any folder it could not delete.

windowsapps-advanced-addons.title: App Add-ons
windowsapps-advanced-addons.description: The optional packages installed against the app - its add-ons / downloadable content - matched by the MainPackageDependency their manifest declares, each removable on its own.

visuals-web.title: Visuals.Web
visuals-web.description: Shared chrome-free WebView2 host (Nexaflow.Visuals.Web): start, navigate, capture, script, and — unlike the code it was extracted from — tear down. Hosts have no toolbar or fallback of their own forced on them, so the Web tab wraps it in browser chrome and the PDF reader wraps it in none.

pdf-ui.title: UI
pdf-ui.description: The reader tab: the rendered page, the resizable document panel beside it, and the file-browser action that opens it.

pdf-render.title: Rendered page surface
pdf-render.description: The document itself, drawn by the shared WebSurface. Edge's own PDF toolbar is deliberately left intact - it already carries page selection, in-page search, zoom and print, and a second set of the same controls would be noise. Nexaflow adds only a panel toggle. No page indicator: there is no API to observe the page the user scrolled to, so any readout would go stale the moment they touched the document.

pdf-panel.title: Document panel
pdf-panel.description: Resizable two-tab side panel fed entirely from the document catalogue, so it fills in without waiting on a content-stream parse. Every value is selectable and copyable; selection stays themed when the window deactivates.

pdf-panel-properties.title: Properties tab
pdf-panel-properties.description: What the PDF says about itself: page count, version, protection, form field count, and every non-empty Information field including the producer/creator/date fields the search path ignores. Empty fields are omitted rather than rendered as a column of dashes.

pdf-panel-toc.title: Contents tab
pdf-panel-toc.description: The document's outline as an indented tree with page numbers, from PdfPig's bookmarks. Clicking a row moves the reader - but only where the embedded renderer honours a page fragment; where it doesn't, the rows render as plain labels rather than links that do nothing.

pdf-open-action.title: As Pdf file action
pdf-open-action.description: IFileAction on /document/pdf/read - a level below Extract Images' /document/pdf so the default-open tie breaks deterministically in the reader's favour. The filemap maps *.pdf to it as a real Extension, which is what makes double-clicking a PDF open Nexaflow rather than falling through to the Windows shell handler.

pdf-page-reading.title: Page text, outline and page images
pdf-page-reading.description: The readers the viewer and the AI share, sitting alongside the frozen search path: per-page text that keeps page identity, the information dictionary and outline with page numbers, and per-page images. Per-page image reads deliberately skip the document-wide dedup that Extract Images needs - asked what is on page 7, 'nothing, you saw that logo on page 1' is simply false.

pdf-reading-order.title: Reading order (layout analysis)
pdf-reading-order.description: The AI's page reads run PdfPig's layout analysis - nearest-neighbour word extraction, Docstrum spatial clustering, then unsupervised block ordering - so a multi-column page reads down each column instead of interleaving them. Falls back to the plain word walk on a page it cannot segment: losing the order beats losing the page. Search keeps the cheap content-stream path, because a sweep is sequential over thousands of files and a bag of words does not need ordering.

pdf-ai.title: AI Integration
pdf-ai.description: A PDF's content is not in the model's context, so the tools are the only way in. Images ride ToolResult.Images, which is what routes them through the shell's existing ImageRecognition shortcut for free; text goes straight back to the conversation model, page-ranged rather than distilled by a second model.

pdf-ai-context.title: Context - get_context
pdf-ai-context.description: Names the file, page count, title/author and outline size, then says plainly that the text is not included and points at the tools. Ready once the panel load finishes, succeeded or failed - a document that will never parse must not block the send forever.

pdf-ai-act.title: Act - client tools
pdf-ai-act.description: Eight read-only tools. Nothing here writes, so none of them stops to ask permission - a confirmation per page would make reading a report unusable.

pdf-ai-act-get-info.title: pdf_get_info
pdf-ai-act-get-info.description: Page count, PDF version, protection, form field count, and every non-empty Information field.

pdf-ai-act-outline.title: pdf_outline
pdf-ai-act-outline.description: The table of contents with page numbers, so the model can jump to the section that matters instead of reading 300 pages.

pdf-ai-act-read-text.title: pdf_read_text
pdf-ai-act-read-text.description: A page range's words with an explicit marker per page. An out-of-range start is an error rather than a silent clamp; a wordless page says so and points at pdf_page_image; hitting the budget names the page it stopped on.

pdf-ai-act-find-text.title: pdf_find_text
pdf-ai-act-find-text.description: Which pages a phrase appears on, with a snippet each - what a model actually wants on a long document instead of paging blindly.

pdf-ai-act-list-images.title: pdf_list_images
pdf-ai-act-list-images.description: Inventory only, no bytes: page, position, pixel size, format, size, and whether it repeats an earlier image. The cheap way to decide what is worth fetching.

pdf-ai-act-get-image.title: pdf_get_image
pdf-ai-act-get-image.description: One embedded image as a ContextImage - a figure, chart or photo on a page.

pdf-ai-act-page-image.title: pdf_page_image
pdf-ai-act-page-image.description: A whole page as a picture. A scanned page IS one full-page image, so it comes straight out of the file at source resolution with no browser involved; anything else has no such image and is photographed from the renderer instead. This is what makes a PDF that is really pages of images readable.

pdf-ai-act-view-page.title: pdf_view_page
pdf-ai-act-view-page.description: Moves the on-screen reader so the user is looking at what the model is talking about. Fails honestly when the renderer won't jump, rather than claiming a view moved that didn't.

pdf-ai-preview.title: Preview - IContextPreview
pdf-ai-preview.description: Not implemented: the AI context hub shows no preview of a pinned PDF yet.

network-page.title: Discovery page
network-page.description: The Network tab: adapters, a Discover button, the device list, and a resizable panel per device. Holds no probe and no action — both arrive as subfeature handles, so a new capability of either kind is a new assembly and never an edit here.

network-page-list.title: Device list
network-page-list.description: One row per device: name, IPv4, IPv6, MAC, which layers found it, and what they said. 'Found by' is the column the page exists for — two independent layers on one row is the graph having decided they are one device.

network-page-panel.title: Device panel
network-page-panel.description: Every fact with its provenance — which layer, how sure, how long ago, and whether anything disagreed. A grid cell can only assert; this is the first place the graph's real shape is visible. Tabbed: Discovery, plus one closable tab per action that has run.

network-page-settings.title: Probe settings
network-page-settings.description: Probes DECLARE their settings (SSDP's mx, search target, whether to fetch descriptions) and nothing renders or persists them, so the defaults are always what runs. DiscoveryRun takes a resolver and is handed none. The declarations are already written for a person AND for the model to read.

network-page-persistence.title: What was here last time
network-page-persistence.description: The graph is thrown away when the tab closes, so IsNew never means anything and the absent/stale machinery never gets to fire. Most of what a discovery tool is worth is over time: what appeared, what went away, what changed hardware.

network-page-cancel.title: Stopping a sweep
network-page-cancel.description: SweepAsync is passed CancellationToken.None. A light sweep is seconds; an opt-in sweep across a /24 will not be, and there is no way to stop one.

network-page-uia.title: Rows a test can reach
network-page-uia.description: No ListItem automation peer survives the shared FileListRowStyle template, so a UI journey can open the tab and run a sweep but cannot click a row. Every selection-dependent behaviour is therefore unverifiable — which is exactly where the inverted-converter bug lived.

network-discovery-arp.title: ARP / neighbour table
network-discovery-arp.description: Layer 0, compiled because it P/Invokes IP Helper and there is no describing that. The only layer that yields a MAC, which is the strongest identity key the graph has. Holds only neighbours this machine has recently exchanged traffic with.

network-discovery-ssdp.title: SSDP / UPnP
network-discovery-ssdp.description: Layer 1, and the first thing in the product to run a protocol description. Writes no octets: the M-SEARCH is values handed to GraphCodec against ssdp.json, replies are read the same way, and the class only knows where SSDP lives and what a header means.

network-discovery-describe.title: Device description
network-discovery-describe.description: The document at LOCATION, fetched through the guard and parsed per UPnP 1.1 §2.3: friendly name, make, model, number, description, serial, presentation URL, and icons. What turns an address into a device with a name.

network-discovery-sweep.title: Address sweep
network-discovery-sweep.description: Ping every address on the prefix so the neighbour table fills, then read it. The only way to find devices that never talk to this machine — phones, a vacuum, anything on wifi that has no reason to. ProbeCost.Sweep: visible to an IDS, opt-in per adapter, and needs the consent story thought through rather than bolted on.

network-discovery-mdns.title: mDNS / DNS-SD
network-discovery-mdns.description: Where phones and most IoT actually announce themselves, and the real test of the architecture: the description already round-trips, so a second document-driven probe should need no new C#. If it does, the engine has not earned its keep.

network-discovery-listen.title: Listening
network-discovery-listen.description: SSDP NOTIFY and mDNS announcements arrive unsolicited, with no request in front of them — a device appearing is an event rather than an answer. ListenMulticastAsync exists and nothing calls it.

network-actions.title: Device actions
network-actions.description: IDeviceAction, mirroring IFileAction: an action declares itself, says whether it applies to the device in hand, and performs. AppliesTo is what makes 'if it has one' a contract rather than a condition in a click handler.

network-action-ping.title: Ping
network-action-ping.description: The only thing on the page speaking in the present tense — everything else is a memory of when a device last was somewhere. Returns facts with a short life, so 'it answered' stops being believed on its own.

network-action-urls.title: Published addresses
network-action-urls.description: Web interface, model page, manufacturer page, service URL — four actions rather than one, because they go to different places and each is offered only where the device published that one.

network-action-portscan.title: Port scan
network-action-portscan.description: TcpConnectAsync exists and nothing calls it. ProbeCost.Heavy, user-initiated, confirmation-gated and budget-bounded — the one action here with a real consent story rather than an obvious answer.

network-action-wol.title: Wake on LAN
network-action-wol.description: A directed broadcast the guard already reasons about — AdapterAddress.DirectedBroadcast exists for it and nothing sends one. Applies to anything with a MAC, which is every device ARP found.

network-graph-topology.title: Topology
network-graph-topology.description: The edges are collected and nothing draws them. DeviceGraph mints a stub for the far end of an edge nothing has described — a real device with an identity and no facts — and the list drops those on purpose, so today they exist and are invisible.

network-graph-eui64.title: Addresses derived from hardware
network-graph-eui64.description: An IPv6 link-local is the MAC with a bit flipped and ff:fe inserted: fe80::6e99:61ff:fe52:a857 IS 6c:99:61:52:a8:57. The graph gets there through the ledger when a probe reports both, and cannot when only one is seen — so the same device can appear twice depending on what answered first.

network-guard-options.title: Network options
network-guard-options.description: The refusal text says 'Turn them back on in Options → Network' and there is no such page. The kill switch, the adapter exclusions and the volume ceilings are all reachable only from code. A message naming a place that does not exist is the worst kind of wrong.

network-guard-audit.title: Audit
network-guard-audit.description: Every send is judged and nothing keeps the verdicts. SendIntent already carries what an audit needs — initiator, source, target, content hash — and a feature that is allowed to talk to the network has to be able to say what it said.

protocol-codec.title: The codec
protocol-codec.description: A demand-driven walk over the protocol graph, keyed by appearance. Facets settle when what they need has settled; there are no passes and nothing back-patches. One description serves both directions, and where they differ it says so.

protocol-corpus.title: The corpus
protocol-corpus.description: Ten real captures assembled before the engine so each defeats it differently, every octet accounted for by exactly one field, verified two independent ways. All ten round-trip. Its wire-shape verdicts are spent; its state-model demands are not.

protocol-definitions.title: Protocol descriptions
protocol-definitions.description: Eleven graphs authored against the RFCs — TCP, NTP, Modbus, MQTT, DHCP, CoAP, mDNS, BACnet, SNMPv2c, TLS and SSDP. They live as test content and one copy ships beside the SSDP probe; where a trusted description should live at run time is not decided.

protocol-empty-runs.title: A run of nothing
protocol-empty-runs.description: A repetition is entered before the edge that goes round again is checked, so a run of zero is unreadable: mDNS cannot read a name that is only the root, SNMP cannot read a two-arc OID or an empty varbind list, TLS cannot read an absent extension block. All legal, none in any capture. The fix is a fork before the first item, which is ordinary vocabulary.

protocol-mdns-response.title: Names that point at names
protocol-mdns-response.description: The mDNS response, which needs a name to be able to end in a compression pointer. Not a cycle — whether to compress is the sender's policy and a width never depends on an offset — but it needs position as a scheduled facet rather than a stamp applied after resolution, plus vocabulary for pointing AT an appearance.

protocol-via-argument.title: A conversion with an argument
protocol-via-argument.description: A field's `via` takes a converter name and nothing else, so minuint — which must be told what a zero comes to — cannot be a field's own conversion. A BACnet Unsigned therefore holds octets and the caller reads them as a number. The stated reason is that a field has nowhere for an argument to come from, which is true of a computed one and not of a literal in the file.

protocol-bidirectional.title: Walkable both ways
protocol-bidirectional.description: Nothing checks that a description can be walked in both directions. A presence that depends on a field further along reads perfectly and deadlocks going out, so a description can be half-right and only the encode side says so — at run time, naming nodes rather than the rule.

protocol-validator-because.title: A validator's own words
protocol-validator-because.description: A validator node carries a `because` that is parsed and never read; only the checks edge's prose reaches a refusal. So a file can explain a range and have the explanation vanish, which is the one thing this format is not supposed to permit.

protocol-length-crosscheck.title: Lengths that check themselves
protocol-length-crosscheck.description: BACnet cross-checks its declared length against what actually arrived, because routers get it wrong. The same check over a span holding a repetition is unsafe: coming in, a set's extent is settled opportunistically as its members close, which for a repeating set can happen after the first round.

protocol-state.title: State
protocol-state.description: The largest deliberate omission. A specification existed, was welded to the deleted document layer, and went with it; only the `state` node kind survives. On the graph model a message and a field are nodes, so legality rules become edges — which is the reason to build it now rather than then. Forty-nine of the corpus's gaps are here and every one is open.

protocol-state-negotiated.title: A peer that grants less
protocol-state-negotiated.description: NINE of the ten corpus protocols independently need it: you ask for something and are given less, per element. BACnet's window size, CoAP's block size, DHCP's lease, MQTT's QoS, NTP's version, TLS's cipher. Nine unrelated specifications arriving at one primitive is the strongest design signal the corpus contains.

protocol-state-timing.title: Saying it again
protocol-state-timing.description: Nine protocols carry a retransmission schedule, a keepalive obligation, a dedup window or a rate limit. MQTT's keepalive is a duty to transmit rather than a peer timeout, and periodic emission is inexpressible. Needs a clock, which nothing here has.

protocol-state-inflight.title: Several at once
protocol-state-inflight.description: Five protocols keep multiple requests outstanding on one socket, told apart only by a token: SNMP's request-id, Modbus's transaction id per unit, BACnet's invoke id. State is one machine per device; there is no per-request container and no bound on how many may be open.

protocol-state-silence.title: Learning nothing
protocol-state-silence.description: Five protocols make silence the only failure signal, and it is ambiguous by construction: a wrong SNMP community is byte-identical to host-down, to a filtered port, and to a lost packet. A timeout that forces one conclusion forces an unsound one — the model needs an outcome that means we did not find out.

protocol-state-epoch.title: A device that restarted
protocol-state-epoch.description: SSDP's BOOTID, SNMP's sysUpTime, a TLS session id: a counter going backwards silently invalidates every fact cached before it, and the evidence arrives in a LATER message. Nothing can express a fact whose validity is scoped to an epoch that something later can retract.

protocol-state-unsolicited.title: Nobody asked
protocol-state-unsolicited.description: mDNS announcements and SSDP NOTIFY arrive with no request in front of them, which is the normal operating mode of both. The model is send-then-expect shaped, so a bare listener has nowhere to live.

protocol-state-tcp.title: Which segment is legal when
protocol-state-tcp.description: RFC 9293 §3.10, the worked case that stalled: legal-in-state plus the transition, both hanging off the message. It loaded and then refused a plain SYN generated from CLOSED, which means the check's view of syn and ack at the message's appearance is not what it looks like. Diagnose that before assuming the shape is wrong.

protocol-authoring.title: Authoring
protocol-authoring.description: Every description here was written by hand against an RFC. The claim is that an AI writes one — and nothing has ever asked it to, so nothing is known about whether the vocabulary is expressible from a specification, what it gets wrong, or how a failure reads.

protocol-review.title: Review
protocol-review.description: A person is supposed to read a description and decide whether to trust it. There is no surface for that: no rendering, no diff against what changed, no way to say yes. A JSON file in a text editor is not a review.

protocol-trust.title: Trust
protocol-trust.description: SendIntent carries a ContentHash whose comment says trust attaches to bytes rather than to a name — an edited document is a different document — and nothing sets it. The guard already refuses a broadcast from an unreviewed draft; nothing tells it which is which.

protocol-hosting.title: Where a description lives
protocol-hosting.description: Descriptions are test content, and the one the SSDP probe uses is a copy shipped beside that assembly. A trusted document a user or an AI added has nowhere to go, no name, and no version.

aichat-context-menu.title: Add-context menu
aichat-context-menu.description: A semi-transparent [+] beside the pinned chips opens the add-context menu; right-clicking the Context Items banner opens the same one. It offers every source the drop target accepts, without a drag: an 'Open tabs' submenu of the workspace's open tabs (this conversation and already-pinned tabs excluded, so no dead entries), then the context-free pages this workspace can create. Pinning an open tab takes no ownership - the tab strip still owns it; pinning a created page does.

aichat-context-collapse.title: Collapse to a summary
aichat-context-collapse.description: A disclosure arrow beside the 'Context Items' label folds the banner to a single line: the label on the left, and the pinned set centred over it as small identity pills - the first three by name, then 'and N more', or 'no context items' when nothing is pinned. Each pill keeps the expanded chip's security-risk badge, so collapsing hides the detail and never the warning. Attachments count as context here (rated Low - a chosen file has no scope behind it), so the summary never under-reports what the model can see. No remove buttons: everything you can DO about the context lives in the expanded chips. Chrome state, not persisted - a conversation reopens expanded.

winfs-action-backing.title: Backing-aware action availability
winfs-action-backing.description: Whether a file/folder action is offered for a virtual path: an action declaring RequiresFullyBackedPath is withheld inside an archive entry (only that one file can be materialised) but allowed under a pass-through mount, where the whole folder is really on disk. FileActionManager filters on VirtualBacking; each shipped action declares its own requirement.

network-ui.title: UI
network-ui.description: The Network tab and the surfaces the user drives it through.

network-functionality.title: Functionality
network-functionality.description: What the feature does behind the page: probing the network, modelling what it finds, decoding the wire, and refusing to send what it shouldn't.

network-ai.title: AI Integration
network-ai.description: Not started. Discovery results and the device graph are the obvious context surface; nothing is wired yet.

product-search-passes.title: Name and source passes
product-search-passes.description: The two passes a query runs, kept apart: NAME through the graph's own ranked search (exact label, then prefix, then substring), and SOURCE through a grep across every code node. The source half is the expensive one, which is why the whole run is off the UI thread and its cap is reported as a floor rather than a total.

winfs-thispc-drives.title: Drive rows
winfs-thispc-drives.description: One row per drive, each resolving its label, capacity, filesystem and HDD/SSD/USB/network/CD type on a background thread and showing a loading or unavailable badge until it answers — so a disconnected network drive degrades to a badge instead of stalling the list.
